question: What changed in the latest Fortnite update?

receipts.question: What changed in the latest Fortnite update?
receipts.answer:
The most recent update the sources give patch notes for is the Treasure Hunters mini-season, covered by IGN on November 2, 2026, which brought a One Piece collaboration, custom Pirate Crews, and a new Battle Pass (800 V-Bucks) [4]. It swaps in a condensed, skull-and-crossbones-shaped 80-player map, Crossbones Isle, with POIs from One Piece such as Windmill Village and Arlong Park [4]. It also adds new Sprites and free items that can drop from chests, including a very rare Pirate Shop Access Token that unlocks the whole Item Shop for free for two weeks, once in 2026 and once in 2027 [4]. Epic later said every player has an equal chance of finding that token, as in any other chest [7].

For creators, Epic's v43.00 ecosystem notes (November 1, 2026) bring Procedural Content Generation to UEFN, take the Progression API out of Experimental, and add more MCP workflows [2].

The previous standard patch, v42.40 on October 15, 2026, added new Loot Hacks and two new Sprites, the Honey Sprite and the One Wish Willow Sprite, along with fixes [1]. I can't confirm from these sources whether anything newer than Treasure Hunters has shipped, since the news page excerpt shows no articles after June 2026 [3].

receipts.question: Which games are coming to Xbox Game Pass this month?
receipts.answer:
Xbox's November 2026 Game Pass wave 1 lineup spans several day-one and mid-month releases, as of the announcement dated November 4, 2026 [1].

Already available or launching at the start of the month:
- Football Manager 27 on PC, and Pit of Goblin [1]
- Gravhounds (Game Preview), listed as available now [1]

- November 11: Hope in the City [1]

question: What are the CDC's current COVID-19 vaccine recommendations for adults?

receipts.question: What are the CDC's current COVID-19 vaccine recommendations for adults?
receipts.answer:
As of the CDC's September 2026 guidance, a 2026-2027 COVID-19 vaccine is recommended for all adults ages 18 years and older [1][4]. The CDC says this applies even if you already had COVID-19, though people who recently had it may consider delaying the dose by 3 months [5]. People who currently have COVID-19 should wait to get vaccinated [5].

The recommended vaccine and number of doses are based on age, vaccination history, and immune status [1]. Adults 65 and older are indicated for 2 doses of the 2026-2027 vaccine, with the second dose 6 months after the first (minimum interval 2 months, or 3 months for Moderna mNexspike) [1]. For ages 12-64, the table shows 1 dose, given at least 8 weeks after the last dose for previously vaccinated people (at least 3 months for mNexspike) [1]. No one vaccine is preferred when more than one recommended, age-appropriate product is available, according to the CDC's overview page [3].

Some sources conflict. The overview and clinical considerations pages still describe individual-based (shared clinical) decision-making for adults and reference 2025-2026 vaccines [2][3]. These appear to be older text, since the 2026-2027 guidance pages, dated September 2026, recommend vaccination for all adults [1][4]. One snippet also notes that, citing legal uncertainties, the CDC says the July 2025 schedule recommendations remain in effect for the 2026-2027 season [6]. That snippet is partial, so I can't say how it fits with the adult recommendation.

Personal decisions, including which vaccine and when, belong with your clinician or pharmacist.

question: Is there a measles outbreak in the United States right now?

receipts.question: Is there a measles outbreak in the United States right now?
receipts.answer:
Yes, the CDC's measles data show ongoing outbreak activity in the United States in 2026. The CDC reports 38 new outbreaks in 2026, and 94% of confirmed cases (2,309 of 2,465) are outbreak-associated, including 1,373 cases from outbreaks that began in 2025 [1]. Note that these figures come from a version of the page labeled as updated August 7, 2026, while a newer version says it was updated November 6, 2026 [1][3]. The newer excerpt doesn't include the 2026 totals, so the current count may be higher than those figures.

The CDC defines an outbreak as 3 or more related cases, and says most U.S. outbreaks are small, usually 6 people or fewer within a household [3]. States have the most current information on local cases and outbreaks, so check your state health department for what is happening near you [3].

question: Who should get a flu shot this season, according to the CDC?

receipts.question: Who should get a flu shot this season, according to the CDC?
receipts.answer:
The CDC says everyone 6 months and older in the United States, with rare exceptions, should get a flu vaccine every season [2]. Its clinical guidance likewise recommends annual vaccination for all people 6 months and older who have no contraindication [6]. For 2026-2027, the CDC says the recommendations from the July 2025 immunization schedule remain in effect [4].

- **Pregnancy:** Studies support the safety of flu shots during any trimester, and vaccination helps protect babies in their first several months, when they are too young to be vaccinated [6].
- **Age 65 and older:** Three vaccines are preferentially recommended: Fluzone High-Dose, Flublok (recombinant), and Fluad (adjuvanted) [5]. If none is available, people in this age group should get any other age-appropriate flu vaccine [2].
- **Under 65:** The CDC has no preference among licensed, age-appropriate vaccines, which can include inactivated, recombinant, or nasal spray options [2].
- **Egg allergy:** The CDC's clinical considerations say people 6 months and older with egg allergy should still get a flu vaccine, and any otherwise appropriate vaccine can be used [4].
- **Timing:** For most people who need one dose, September or October is ideal [4].

Some groups, such as pregnant women and people with certain health conditions, should not receive the nasal spray [3][5]. Personal decisions about which vaccine is right for you belong with a clinician.

question: What did Apple report in its most recent quarterly earnings?

receipts.question: What did Apple report in its most recent quarterly earnings?
receipts.answer:
Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter 2026 results on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, with revenue of $114.48 billion (up 12% from $102.5 billion a year earlier) and EPS of $2.10, both above analyst estimates of $113.39 billion and $1.99 [2]. - **Margin:** Gross margin was 47.9% vs. 47.5% estimated [2]. Tariff refunds added 5 cents to EPS [2].
- **Guidance:** Apple expects December-quarter revenue growth of 7% to 10%, above the 6.1% average estimate, but a gross margin of 45% to 46%, below the 46.3% estimate [2]. The stock slid 3% in extended trading [2].

Apple said memory costs were higher than in the June quarter [2].

question: What is the current federal funds rate target range?

receipts.question: What is the current federal funds rate target range?
receipts.answer:
The federal funds target range is 3-3/4 to 4 percent, as of the FOMC's October 28, 2026 statement [2]. The FOMC held it there at its October 28, 2026 meeting by a 10–2 vote [2]. The range was set at the September 15–16, 2026 meeting, when the Committee raised it by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent [3]. At the October meeting, Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack dissented because they preferred another 1/4-point increase [2].

This is general information, not personal financial advice. Decisions about your own money are worth discussing with a qualified professional.

question: What is the latest news on NASA's Artemis program?

receipts.question: What is the latest news on NASA's Artemis program?
receipts.answer:
NASA's latest update, given on Oct. 23, 2026, says it is on a path to land Americans on the Moon in 2028, with Artemis III as a 2027 Earth-orbit test flight and Artemis IV as the first landing mission [7][8].

- **Artemis III (2027):** Four astronauts will fly on Orion for a planned 14-day mission in Earth orbit. They will test rendezvous and docking with lander test articles from Blue Origin and SpaceX [7]. Blue Origin's test lander launches first, then SLS launches Orion to dock with it. SpaceX then launches a Version 3 Starship test article, and Orion undocks from Blue Moon and docks with Starship [7].
- **Hardware progress:** NASA says Artemis III hardware is on track, with processing timelines cut by about half [7]. The Orion crew and service modules were joined on July 30 [2]. NASA also selected SpaceX's Starlink laser terminals to deliver imagery from Orion on that mission [2].
- **Landers:** NASA updated its contracts with Blue Origin and SpaceX, and neither company is assigned to a specific lunar landing mission [3]. Based on lander readiness, NASA will decide which company is first to land astronauts in 2028, with a second landing opportunity to follow [3]. Both companies must fly an uncrewed demonstration before the crewed missions [3].
- **Mission design changes:** Landers and Orion will no longer meet in a near-rectilinear halo orbit. They will rendezvous in an orbit that differs for each partner [3]. Blue Origin's plan uses an elliptical polar orbit and defers propellant transfer [3].
- **Artemis II background:** The crewed lunar flyby launched April 1, and the crew has since returned to Houston [2].

question: What are the most recent discoveries from the James Webb Space Telescope?

receipts.question: What are the most recent discoveries from the James Webb Space Telescope?
receipts.answer:
Two Webb-related results in these sources, dated in early November 2026, are a new starlight-removal technique [5][6] and a survey of distant icy objects [3].

- **Hidden exoplanet (reported November 10, 2026):** Researchers built a "digital twin" of Webb's NIRCam, a method called FLIP, that removes starlight from existing images and was two to 15 times more sensitive than conventional approaches in tests on known planets [5]. It exposed a previously hidden exoplanet in existing observations [5]. Scientific American (November 4) describes a Nature study testing FLIP on three star systems, where it captured the giant planet 51 Eridani b, which was not previously visible at the wavelengths Webb detects [6]. The two accounts differ in wording: one calls the planet "previously hidden," the other calls it a "known giant planet" newly seen in Webb data [5][6].
- **Distant icy bodies (November 1, 2026):** Hubble and Webb studied 27 small trans-Neptunian objects and found they appear to have changed little since the solar system's beginnings, while Webb found fewer tiny objects than expected [3].
- **Organic molecules (February 2026, older):** Webb detected benzene, methane and the methyl radical in the galaxy IRAS 07251-0248, the first detection of the methyl radical outside the Milky Way [2]. The evidence points to cosmic rays as a key factor in releasing these molecules [2].

question: Is 2026 on track to be one of the hottest years on record?

receipts.question: Is 2026 on track to be one of the hottest years on record?
receipts.answer:
Copernicus and NOAA both point to 2026 most likely ranking as the second-hottest year on record [1][5]. Copernicus said on November 6, 2026 that 2026 will "most likely" be the second-hottest year, with a 20% chance of tying or exceeding 2024's record [1]. NOAA's outlook likewise says 2026 will very likely rank among the five warmest years, with the highest probabilities favoring second-warmest [5]. The WMO found that January–September 2026 averaged about 1.47 °C above preindustrial, below 2024's record of 1.55 °C, but it expects the final 2026 figure to rise because of El Niño [4].

Copernicus says 2026 is "virtually certain" to exceed 1.5 °C above preindustrial [1]. Scientific American cites a projection of 1.52 °C for 2026 and says it could set a record, though 2027 is virtually certain to take the crown [2]. The WMO says El Niño typically has its greatest effect on global temperatures in the year after it develops [4].

question: What is the current federal minimum wage in the United States?

receipts.question: What is the current federal minimum wage in the United States?
receipts.answer:
The federal minimum wage under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) is $7.25 per hour for covered non-exempt workers in the United States, as of the U.S. Department of Labor's July 1, 2026 table [3][4]. The same table lists the federal minimum cash wage for tipped employees at $2.13, with a maximum tip credit of $5.12 [3]. If an employee is subject to both state and FLSA minimum wage laws, they are entitled to the higher one, and many states set higher rates [3][4].

A separate rate under Executive Order 13658 applies to certain types of federal contracts entered into between January 1, 2015, and January 29, 2022, that were not renewed or extended on or after January 30, 2022 [1][2]. That rate is $13.65 per hour since May 11, 2026, and is set to rise to $14.05 on January 6, 2027, per the newer October 2026 notice [1][2].

A bill to raise the federal minimum wage (H.R.8555, the Living Wage For All Act) was introduced in April 2026 and referred to committee. The sources show no enactment [5].

This covers U.S. federal law only; state and local rules differ. For how this applies to a specific situation, consult a licensed lawyer.

question: Do US citizens need ETIAS authorization to visit Europe now?

receipts.question: Do US citizens need ETIAS authorization to visit Europe now?
receipts.answer:
No, not yet as far as the sources show. ETIAS is planned to start operations in the last quarter of 2026 [4][8]. The EU's travel site says ETIAS is currently not in operation and no applications are being collected, and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch [8]. That page is undated, so it may be out of date.

The sources conflict on how firm the requirement is. The State Department's Iceland advisory (last updated May 14, 2026) says U.S. citizens must apply for ETIAS approval beginning in the last 3 months of 2026 [3]. Its Europe guide says only that ETIAS plans to launch in late 2026 and that U.S. citizens currently do not need an electronic travel authorization for the Schengen Area or EU [1]. question: What are the current TSA rules for liquids in carry-on bags?

receipts.question: What are the current TSA rules for liquids in carry-on bags?
receipts.answer:
Under the 3-1-1 rule, each passenger may carry liquids, gels and aerosols in containers of 3.4 ounces (100 milliliters) or less, all within one quart-size bag [7]. Common items covered include toothpaste, shampoo, conditioner, mouthwash and lotion [7]. Hand sanitizer also falls under the rule, limited to 3.4-ounce (100 mL) containers [8].

There are exceptions. Medically necessary liquids, medications and creams may exceed 3.4 ounces in your carry-on [7]. You must declare them to TSA officers at the checkpoint for inspection, and they should be removed from your bag and placed in a bin [6]. Liquids associated with nebulizers are also exempt from the 3-1-1 rule [5][6].

In lanes with CT scanners, passengers do not need to remove their travel-sized 3-1-1 liquids from the bag [3]. The sources don't give dates for these rules, so I can't say how recently they were confirmed, and the excerpts don't cover the rules for baby food, breast milk or formula beyond noting that special instructions exist [1].

question: Do US citizens need a visa to visit Japan for tourism?

receipts.question: Do US citizens need a visa to visit Japan for tourism?
receipts.answer:
No, US citizens don't need a visa for tourism in Japan; they can enter visa-free for stays of up to 90 days [1][7]. The State Department's Japan advisory (issued September 28, 2026) lists tourist or business "visa free" stays up to 90 days [1]. A source dated October 2026 says Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs lists the United States among its visa-exempt countries, with a standard 90-day stay granted on landing [7].

Working in Japan on a tourist visa is illegal [1]. Visa-free arrival gives Temporary Visitor status, which covers tourism, recuperation, sports, visiting relatives, short courses and business liaison [7].

Related changes as of October 2026:
- **Departure tax:** The international tourist tax rose to 3,000 yen per departure on July 1, 2026, and is normally included in the airfare [7].
- **Pre-entry authorization:** Japan plans a pre-travel authorization system for visa-exempt visitors, but no exact start date has been announced [7].
- **Visit Japan Web:** Travelers are advised to register before arrival to submit customs and immigration information [2].

I can't confirm from these sources whether Japan has set a minimum passport validity requirement for US citizens. Check the Immigration Bureau of Japan for landing procedures [1].

question: What internal temperature does the USDA recommend for cooking chicken?

receipts.question: What internal temperature does the USDA recommend for cooking chicken?
receipts.answer:
The USDA recommends cooking chicken to an internal temperature of 165°F [1][6]. The Serious Eats article describes this as the official USDA guidance and the "simplest, safest, most foolproof recommendation" [1]. A USDA FSIS page from May 2026 also lists 165°F for poultry and advises checking with a food thermometer [6]. FSIS's November 2025 turkey guidance likewise says to confirm 165°F in the thickest part of the breast, innermost part of the thigh, and innermost part of the wing [5].

CDC says the same, advising 165°F for chicken and for all poultry [3][4].

Serious Eats argues that chicken can be safe below 165°F if held at a lower temperature for long enough, for example 150°F for 4.2 minutes. It cites FSIS Appendix A tables for those times, but it also says that anyone cooking for people at higher risk of foodborne illness should stick to 165°F [1].

question: When does the 2027-28 FAFSA open, and what changed?

receipts.question: When does the 2027-28 FAFSA open, and what changed?
receipts.answer:
The 2027–28 FAFSA launched to the public on September 23, 2026, ahead of the October 1 statutory deadline [1][6]. The Department called it the earliest launch in program history for the second year in a row [1][6]. Federal aid applications can't be submitted earlier than October 1, 2026, per the form itself, and must be received by June 30, 2028 [2]. The sources don't explain how the September 23 launch fits with that October 1 language.

What changed or is highlighted for 2027–28:
- Questions and instructions were rewritten in clearer language [1][4].
- Students can invite a contributor by text message as well as email [1]. The Department's blog also describes QR-code invitations for a parent or spouse [4].
- Returning students' data will be pre-populated from prior FAFSAs "later this fall" [1][4]. The specifications guide says the renewal implementation date had not been confirmed when it was published in September 2026 [3].
- The Department says features from the previous cycle carry forward: real-time eligibility results, reuse of parent information across siblings, instant verification for new StudentAid.gov accounts, and the earnings indicator [1][4].
- The specifications guide notes significant changes to questions on both the online and PDF forms [3].

question: What is the average tuition at US public four-year colleges this year?

receipts.question: What is the average tuition at US public four-year colleges this year?
receipts.answer:
The average published in-state tuition and fees at US public four-year colleges for 2026-27 is $12,290, according to the College Board's Trends in College Pricing and Student Aid 2026 report [6][7]. Out-of-state students at public four-year colleges face an average published price of $32,730 [7]. After grant aid and tax benefits, first-time, full-time in-state students pay an estimated net average of $1,920 for tuition and fees [6].

Older figures are lower: Coursera cites $11,950 for 2025-26 public four-year tuition [3], and U.S. News data cited by Coursera gives $11,371 for in-state public tuition that year [1]. The 2026-27 figures are the newest, and the College Board numbers come from reports released in late 2026 [6][7].

question: What's new in the latest version of Blender?

receipts.question: What's new in the latest version of Blender?
receipts.answer:
Blender 5.3, released November 10, 2026, is the latest version, and its headline feature is native support for 3D Gaussian Splats. [1] Splats can be imported from PLY and SPZ files as point clouds, edited with Geometry Nodes, and relit and rendered in Workbench, EEVEE and Cycles. [1]

Other changes include:
- **Assets and extensions:** Asset Libraries can be shared as extensions, and the Extensions platform accepts Asset Libraries containing Public Domain (CC0) assets. [1]
- **Graphics and hardware:** A new DLSS denoiser for the viewport on NVIDIA GPUs, native support for NVIDIA RTX Spark devices on Windows 11, and Vulkan as the default backend on Windows (except ARM) and Linux. Workbench can also use hardware raytraced shadows on Metal and Vulkan. [1]
- **Grease Pencil:** Selection tools in Draw Mode, a new Carver Tool for boolean subtraction, and a Fill tool that can fill many regions at once. [1]
- **Video Sequencer:** A full ripple editing framework, a rewritten blade tool, and initial OpenTimelineIO support. [1]
- **Projects:** A new optional project system that makes Blender aware of context beyond the open .blend file. [1]
- **Animation & Rigging:** Operators to copy and paste world-space animation and to convert rotation modes, plus friendlier playback. [1]

question: What is the US Copyright Office's current position on AI-generated art?

receipts.question: What is the US Copyright Office's current position on AI-generated art?
receipts.answer:
The Office's position is that copyright requires human authorship, and that copyright does not extend to purely AI-generated material, while the original expression of a human author in a work that includes AI-generated material can be protected [5][2]. Its January 2025 copyrightability report (Part 2) affirmed that copyright does not extend to purely AI-generated material, or to material where human control over the expressive elements is insufficient to constitute authorship [5]. The same report states that AI tools used to assist rather than stand in for human creativity do not affect protection for the output, and that copyright protects the human author's original expression even if the work also includes AI-generated material [2].

In practice, the Office has registered hundreds of works incorporating AI-generated material, with registration covering the human author's contribution [2]. In litigation over a Midjourney-generated image, the Office said it could have registered the claim if the applicant had excluded the material he did not author [2]. The Office also says that randomness in Midjourney outputs illustrates how much expression is attributable to the tool rather than the user [2].

The human-authorship requirement was confirmed by the D.C. Circuit in Thaler v. Perlmutter, and the Supreme Court declined to review it, as described in the Register's May 12, 2026 Senate testimony [5]. The Office's analysis is described as depending on the circumstances of each work's creation [4].
